headline: Approved $1.2 million for Memorial Field design and permitting, 12-3; approved several zoning and parking ordinances; referred Noyes and Cypress Streets traffic ordinance.
summary: Members approved $1.2 million for final design and permitting at Memorial Field, funded by $600,000 in bonds and notes and $600,000 from Concord School District. Several members raised concerns about cost-sharing, funding sources, and the need for a written agreement with the school district. Members also approved several zoning and parking ordinances and referred a Noyes and Cypress Streets traffic ordinance to committees.
decisions: Approved the September 14, 2026 draft meeting minutes, with one dissenting vote.
Referred a request for a flashing pedestrian light at Rumford and Centre Street to the Traffic Operations Committee.
Referred a request for an extended walk signal and an exclusive pedestrian phase at Centre and Green Streets to the Traffic Operations Committee.
Referred a request to address recurring vandalism of City property to the Recreation and Parks Advisory Committee and the Public Safety Board.
Moved to set a $70,589.24 opioid settlement fund transfer for a November 9, 2026 public hearing.
Moved to set an $8,300 Golf Course Improvement Reserve for a November 9, 2026 public hearing.
Moved to set the petition to restore Oak Hill Road to the Merrimack Valley School District for a November 9, 2026 public hearing.
Moved to set the change of the Administrative Coordinator position in Human Resources to full-time for a November 9, 2026 public hearing.
Moved to set the demolition review ordinance amendment for a November 9, 2026 public hearing.
Approved $1,200,000 for Memorial Field final design and permitting, including $600,000 in bonds and notes, by a 12-3 roll call.
Approved an ordinance changing the parking time limit on the north side of Merrimack Street in Penacook.
Approved a zoning ordinance amending Article 28-7 on access, circulation, parking, and loading, with no dissenting votes.
Approved a zoning ordinance amending Section 28-8-5(d) on replacing certain nonconforming residential structures, with no dissenting votes.
Approved a zoning ordinance updating flood insurance study references in the zoning map section, with no dissenting votes.
Approved a zoning ordinance updating the lists of arterial and collector streets, with no dissenting votes.
Approved fire, building, and housing code ordinance changes, with no dissenting votes.
Approved a resolution appropriating $23,397 in Edward Byrne grant funds for law enforcement programs, with no dissenting votes.
Kept tabled the ordinance to modify parking requirements on School Street between Pine and Liberty Streets.
Denied a motion to set the Noyes and Cypress Streets restricted-access ordinance for a December public hearing.
Referred the Noyes and Cypress Streets ordinance to the City Solicitor's Office, TPAC, and TOC, with a public hearing planned for December, with one dissenting vote.
Approved the Rules Committee's ethics complaint form as a proposed change to the Rules of the City Council, with one dissenting vote.

26I. Resolution appropriating the sum of $1,200,000 in the Memorial Field Project (CIP

#557) for Final Design and Permitting, authorizing the issuance of General Obligation Bonds and Notes in the sum of $600,000, and accepting the sum of $600,000 in donations from the Concord School District for this purpose; together with a report from the Parks and Recreation Director. (Public testimony received.)

Action: Parks and Recreation Director David Gill provided an update on the

Memorial Field master planning process, which began in June 2023 as a joint initiative of the City Council and the Concord School Board. Following public meetings, student input, and approximately ten Joint City-School Committee meetings, a revised plan was presented on September 3, 2026.

Mr. Gill explained the proposed plan generally maintains the existing field layout while addressing drainage and field conditions and improving fencing, lighting, the bus lane, and parking. Approximately 55 additional parking spaces are proposed, however, the improvements would not fully resolve parking shortages during events. The committee recommended a $1.2 million investment, to be shared equally by the City and Concord School District, for final design, construction documents, and required state permitting. He noted the request does not include construction costs. The City Council had tabled its decision in December 2025 to allow further review of costs and funding options.

Mr. Gill discussed potential grant opportunities, including the Land and Water Conservation Fund and the Outdoor Recreation Legacy Partnership program, however, the City and Concord School District must first determine how to fund construction and address future operating expenses. Final design and permitting are expected to take approximately 12 months, with construction completion potentially occurring in 2028 under an optimistic timeline, although 2029 is considered more realistic. He noted that project reports and Committee meeting minutes are available on the City's website.

City Manager Aspell reviewed three potential funding sources for the Memorial Field project. The Recreation Reserve currently has a balance of $879,600, of which $350,000 is committed to projects approved for 2027, leaving approximately $529,600 potentially available. He noted that these funds may already be anticipated for other purposes, including Community Center bond payments and the golf course clubhouse project. The Impact Fee Fund has a current balance of approximately $96,000, of which $86,000 is uncommitted. He noted Memorial Field is considered a citywide project, and funds from any of the four impact fee sectors may be used, while additional revenue from future housing development may increase the balance over time. Additionally, approximately $140,000 may remain from the $385,000 appropriated through the Capital Project Fund for the removal of the bleachers and site cleanup. However, final invoices have not been received and the project has not been closed out and recommended waiting before considering these funds available for other uses.

City Manager Aspell emphasized that these three funding sources could be considered for design or construction, subject to applicable requirements and other commitments. He also encouraged the Council to consider the City's long-term financial obligations and anticipated expenses over the next 20 years when determining how to allocate available funds.

During Council discussion, Councilor Kurtz clarified that the proposed 50/50 cost-sharing arrangement between the City and Concord School District applied only to the $1.2 million for final design and permitting. Mr. Gill confirmed that no agreements had been made regarding the financing of subsequent project phases and that any future funding arrangements would require further consideration by the Council.

Councilor Kretovic noted that efforts to secure the Concord School District’s participation in Memorial Field improvements had been ongoing for more than 15 years. City Manager Aspell acknowledged that discussions had been underway for many years.

Councilor Brown questioned the history of deferred maintenance at Memorial Field and asked about responsibility for maintaining the facility before its transfer to the Parks and Recreation Department in 2012. City Manager Aspell explained that maintenance and capital improvements had historically been managed through the City’s budgeting and capital improvement prioritization process through City Council, with other parks and recreational facilities receiving higher priority in previous years. Councilor Brown raised concerns about the timing of the request in relation to other major municipal projects and existing debt obligations.

Councilor Kalob asked about the project phasing and drainage improvements. Mr. Gill confirmed that drainage improvements were included in Phase One across the natural grass fields and baseball field. He noted that drainage problems had persisted throughout his 28 years working with the City and that portions of the field had experienced drainage issues since the 1990s.

Councilor Sekou questioned whether the project could be designed in stages to reduce the initial design cost, noting that the first phase represented a substantial portion of the overall project. Mr. Gill explained that the $1.2 million estimate covered final design and permitting for the full master plan. He stated that completing the full design would strengthen the City’s competitiveness for grant funding and allow the City to proceed with construction procurement once funding was secured. He was not aware of an alternative partial-design approach that would provide the same benefits.

Councilor Kalob asked how the Concord School District was financing its $600,000 share. City Manager Aspell confirmed that the City had received a $600,000 check from the Concord School District but did not know how the payment was financed.

Councilor Foote asked whether the $1.2 million design and permitting amount represented a not-to-exceed limit. Mr. Gill confirmed that it did and stated that the goal was to complete the work for less than the approved amount.

Mayor Champlin opened the public testimony.

Emma Sisti, Ward 6, a lifelong Concord resident, expressed support for improvements to Memorial Field, citing its importance to local schools, youth sports, and the community. As president of Concord Crush Youth Lacrosse, a nonprofit serving approximately 150 children in kindergarten through eighth grade, she explained that poor drainage and limited field availability restrict practices and competitions. Because the fields are often unusable until May, teams must schedule away games early in the season and compress their home schedules. She noted that wet conditions limit safe field use, affecting athletic development and potentially discouraging students from continuing sports in high school. She also highlighted the deteriorated track, which she said is inadequate for hosting high school meets, and encouraged improvements that would support competitive athletic events, attract visitors, generate revenue, and expand recreational opportunities.

In response to Councilors’ questions, Ms. Sisti clarified that Concord Crush Youth Lacrosse is an independent nonprofit serving youth through eighth grade and coordinates field use with the Parks and Recreation Department. She expressed support for turf fields to allow earlier-season use but acknowledged that adequate drainage and maintenance could also make natural grass viable. She added that longstanding deterioration and limitations on field size and access have constrained athletic use.

Roy Schweiker, resident of Ward 4, expressed concern about the proposed Memorial Field Master Plan’s cost and priorities, arguing that the City should consider competing financial obligations, including water infrastructure improvements. He questioned the extent to which the project would benefit the City compared with the Concord School District and recommended that the Concord School District contribute a greater share of the costs. He also questioned the need to hire a consultant to develop the plan, raised concerns about artificial turf and potential safety issues, and advocated for a scaled-back project.

Katrina Malone, resident of Ward 10, expressed support for improvements to Memorial Field, drawing on her involvement with the high school football and lacrosse booster clubs and participation in community softball. She described recurring drainage problems, field closures, and limited playability that require practices and games to be relocated to other facilities. She also highlighted hazards caused by uneven pavement and raised asphalt along access routes, which she said pose risks to students, parents, and older visitors. Ms. Malone emphasized that Memorial Field serves student athletes and the broader community. In response to a Councilor’s question, she confirmed that she communicates concerns to school personnel and grounds staff.

Alan Robitas, resident of Ward 5, opposed advancing the project before the City and Concord School District establish a written agreement defining their respective financial responsibilities. Drawing on his business experience, he argued that proceeding with project development before determining the cost-sharing arrangement and final budget would be premature. He questioned the City’s priorities in light of other major expenditures and urged the Council to proceed cautiously, establish funding responsibilities, and account for competing municipal needs. In response to a Councilor’s question, he reiterated that the cost-sharing arrangement should be resolved before the project advances, warning that the City could otherwise assume a disproportionate share of the expense.

Alique Valeras, Ward 5 resident and Concord High School sophomore, described challenges affecting the marching band and cross-country and track teams. He reported that uneven pavement and raised asphalt areas along the route to Memorial Field create tripping hazards for marching band members. He also cited inadequate seating arrangements for the band and student section, which limit communication and participation during football games. Regarding track facilities, he noted that the condemned track has forced athletes to seek alternative locations for workouts and that puddles and exposed roots continue to create difficulties. He expressed support for improvements that would allow students to use the facilities safely and effectively.

Bob Washburn, Ward 8 resident, supported addressing Memorial Field’s deteriorated condition but raised concerns about project planning, financing, and procurement. He questioned proceeding with architectural design before the Council approves the project footprint and recommended that the City and Concord School District establish written agreements specifying their respective financial commitments before entering into further agreements. He also questioned borrowing $600,000 for the City’s share of the proposed $1.2 million design and permitting phase when reserve funds might be available. Mr. Washburn urged the City to disclose relevant financial information and conduct a publicly advertised, competitive procurement process for the architectural contract. He also raised concerns about the long-term maintenance costs of artificial turf and emphasized the need to resolve the cost-sharing arrangement. He reiterated that the need for improvements was compelling but that the project should proceed with appropriate financial safeguards.

Courtney Levesque, resident of Ward 4, expressed support for the redevelopment of Memorial Field and improvements to the City’s athletic facilities. As a parent-teacher association member and Vice President of the Concord Capitals Youth Football and Cheer Program, she described recurring challenges involving field availability, weather-related cancellations, inadequate lighting, and schedule changes affecting youth athletes and school programs. She noted that these issues create transportation and scheduling difficulties for families and participating teams. She also highlighted the program’s efforts to provide scholarships and ensure that financial constraints do not exclude participants. Ms. Levesque emphasized the importance of reliable, accessible athletic facilities to youth sports and the broader community. In response to Councilors’ questions, she clarified that the Concord Capitals is an independent nonprofit youth football program that serves as a feeder program for the high school team.

Jennifer Chase, resident of Ward 2, expressed concern that Penacook residents could be required to contribute to a project that primarily benefits Concord School District students and facilities. Drawing on her experiences growing up in the Merrimack Valley area and later living in Penacook, she contrasted the athletic facilities available in Concord with those available to students in her former community. She clarified that her concern was not necessarily with the proposed improvements but with the fairness of the funding arrangement, given differences in facility access and use. Ms. Chase urged the City to establish and disclose cost-sharing percentages before proceeding with design and permitting. In response to the Mayor, she stated that a proposed 50/50 split for the design phase did not resolve concerns about the allocation of future project costs. She suggested that costs should reflect the actual use of individual facilities and questioned why negotiations remained unresolved after years of discussion and a petition signed by more than 600 residents.

Madeline Mineau, resident of Ward 4, urged the Council to proceed promptly with design and permitting for Memorial Field improvements. Speaking as a resident and parent of student athletes, rather than on behalf of the Concord School Board, she described the facility’s extensive community use, including soccer tournaments, baseball games, and recreational running. She argued that a 50/50 split for the current phase would result in Concord School District taxpayers funding more than 95% of the project costs, based on the distribution of property values across the City. She also cited missed seasons, off-site practices, and the inability to host home track meets as evidence of the impact of deteriorated facilities on students and the community. Ms. Mineau encouraged the Council to advance the design and permitting phase. During the discussion, she acknowledged that she had not formally reported field conditions but had heard concerns from coaches and observed the facility’s condition firsthand.

Jessica Wheeler-Russell, Ward 2 resident, speaking as a private citizen and clarifying that her remarks did not represent the Merrimack Valley School Board, urged the Council not to proceed with the proposed 50/50 cost split for the Memorial Field Master Plan and permitting phase before establishing a fair funding agreement between the City and Concord School District. She expressed concern that approving successive phases under the same arrangement could make it more difficult to negotiate a different allocation for construction. She argued that Penacook residents contribute to Memorial Field through City taxes while also funding Merrimack Valley School District facilities, creating an inequitable burden. Ms. Wheeler-Russell cited approximately 670 petition signatures opposed to the proposed arrangement. She reported facility-use data indicates that Concord School District accounts for a substantial share of usage at several Memorial Field facilities. She also cited 2026 New Hampshire Department of Education data indicating that 43% of Penacook students qualified for free or reduced-price lunch, compared with 32% in Concord School District and 24% statewide. She clarified that her opposition was not to repairing Memorial Field but to the proposed cost allocation and scope of improvements. She urged the Council to delay or condition the appropriation until the City and Concord School District negotiate a fair cost-sharing arrangement and distinguish essential improvements from discretionary enhancements.

In response to Councilors’ questions, Ms. Wheeler-Russell expressed support for a usage-based allocation and stated that a higher contribution from Concord School District for facilities it uses most frequently would be more equitable than a 50/50 or 60/40 split. She questioned whether current usage data accurately reflected demand, given the facility’s deteriorated condition and the relocation of activities to other sites. She also stated that additional information was needed to assess school funding allocations and reiterated her concerns about using Recreation Reserve Funds before outstanding issues were resolved.

Tracy Bricchi, Ward 1 resident, expressed support for Ms. Wheeler-Russell’s concerns, noting that Merrimack Valley School District pays the full cost of maintaining its athletic facilities while allowing Concord School District teams to use them without charge. She stated that Memorial Field’s drainage and playing-surface problems had persisted for decades, recalling similar waterlogged conditions when she participated in the Concord High School marching band nearly 50 years earlier. Ms. Bricchi opposed making a funding decision before resolving broader questions about the project and cost-sharing arrangement and raised concerns about using recreation reserve funds for the current appropriation. She also requested an apology from the Mayor regarding a previous response to public testimony. Mayor Champlin apologized for any offense caused and stated that none had been intended.

Meredith Cooley, resident of Ward 5, expressed strong support for renovating Memorial Field, describing it as a central gathering place for the Concord community. Drawing on her experiences as a resident and parent, she recalled using the field for walks, teaching her children to play tennis, running the track, attending fireworks, and watching high school sporting events. She described the facility as the heart of the community, where residents of all ages gather and build relationships. Noting that her son now plays freshman football, she emphasized the value of athletic events in bringing generations together and the importance of sports in promoting physical activity, reducing screen time, and connecting children with supportive adult mentors and coaches. She also encouraged young people attending the meeting to speak publicly, emphasizing that their voices matter even when their remarks are not prepared. Ms. Cooley urged the Council to move forward with the renovation as an investment in children and future generations.

Ms. Cooley also highlighted community programs that use Memorial Field to provide children with opportunities for recreation, connection, and personal growth. Citing the Spark program, Concord Capitals, and Girls on the Run, she described how community partnerships provide youth with athletic opportunities, scholarships, supportive relationships, and pathways to further participation, including employment as sports officials. She noted that the track’s condition has created uncertainty about where Girls on the Run could hold its spring 5K. In response to Councilor Schultz, Cooley explained that independent nonprofit sports organizations complement school athletics by helping children develop skills, discover talents, and access additional opportunities and adult role models. Councilor Sekou thanked Cooley for her testimony and her advocacy for children in the community.

Mona Lisa Eaton, resident, emphasized the importance of safe athletic facilities and the role of sports in helping young people pursue educational and personal opportunities. She noted that student athletes, including wrestlers, had gone on to compete in college and expressed hope that young people would have similar opportunities while participating safely in sports. In response to Councilors’ comments, she acknowledged that renters contribute to the community and agreed that all children should have equitable access to safe recreational facilities, regardless of their families’ financial circumstances. She explained that her grandson could not afford to participate in football and soccer until the Concord Capitals and other organizations provided scholarships or financial assistance. Eaton expressed concern that children from lower-income families should not have to risk injury because they lack access to better facilities. In response to Mayor Champlin, she agreed that athletics, band, and other extracurricular activities can provide young people with positive opportunities, help them develop communication skills and pursue a more positive future.

Mason Romboldi, Raider Agan, and Parker Price, students and members of the Concord High School athletics program, described concerns about the condition and safety of Memorial Field. Mason, a sophomore who participates in track and football, characterized the track as unusable because of cracks, uneven grass, and other deterioration, explaining that track athletes must practice in school hallways, including performing block starts indoors. Raider, who has played football at Memorial Field since sixth grade, described injuries associated with holes in the playing surface and noted that the field’s uneven, raised center could pose additional risks. Parker echoed these concerns.

Mason Romboldi also described the potential impact of the deteriorated track on student participation, citing a highly accomplished triple jumper who had left Concord High School and suggesting that inadequate training facilities may have contributed to the decision. He expressed concern that other talented athletes could similarly seek opportunities elsewhere if they cannot access suitable facilities. Councilors thanked the students for sharing their experiences and emphasized the importance of providing safe, appropriate facilities for student athletes.

Tim Latorra, Ward 7 resident and Concord High School’s Head Basketball Coach, expressed support for improvements to Memorial Field, emphasizing the importance of safety for student athletes and the broader community. He described a student athlete who sustained a knee injury after stepping into a pothole on the football field, noting that the injury continued to affect the student during his college football career. Mr. Latorra highlighted the facility’s use by organizations beyond Concord School District, including adult softball, Little League baseball, Concord Crush Youth Lacrosse, and Fit for a Cause, which holds boot camps at Memorial Field to raise funds for people affected by cancer. He recalled the track’s past use by residents for exercise and argued that the facility’s current condition was inconsistent with Concord’s role as the capital city. He urged the Council to treat the project as a necessary investment rather than defer improvements further, emphasizing the opportunity to improve safety and expand recreational opportunities for students and community members.

Stephen Largy, Athletic Director at Concord High School, described Memorial Field as a valued community facility whose deteriorated condition has affected student athletics and Concord School District’s ability to host events. He highlighted the traditions associated with Friday night football games and expressed concern that visiting teams and athletic administrators increasingly viewed the facility’s condition unfavorably. He noted that the lack of adequate bleachers, a usable track, and appropriate visiting-team changing facilities has limited Concord School District’s ability to host competitions and accommodate student athletes. With Rundlett Middle School unavailable for use, the City and Concord School District have worked together to find alternative locations for games and practices, including sharing rented lighting equipment between Martin Park and Memorial Field. Mr. Largy emphasized that the facilities’ limitations have required increasingly creative scheduling and coordination with community organizations.

Mr. Largy described the City and Concord School District’s ongoing collaboration and noted that Concord School District’s $600,000 contribution toward the proposed design and permitting phase was made in good faith under the existing joint-use agreement. While acknowledging that he could not speak on behalf of the Concord School Board regarding future cost-sharing arrangements, he urged the Council to advance the project as an initial step toward addressing the facility’s condition. He emphasized the importance of improving safety, supporting student athletes and coaches, and preserving opportunities for community use.

Chris Galbraith, a Ward 5 resident and part owner of North Branch Construction, expressed support for advancing the proposed $1.2 million design and permitting phase for Memorial Field. Drawing on his experience as a local business owner and parent of three sons who have participated in youth, middle school, and high school sports, he described the facility’s condition as embarrassing and expressed concern about the limited seating and viewing opportunities for families attending football games. He noted that attendance can reach approximately 1,500 people, while seating accommodates only an estimated 200 to 300, making it difficult for parents and grandparents to watch their children compete. He also cited the potential costs and consequences of athletic injuries and argued that construction costs are likely to increase if improvements are delayed. Mr. Galbraith characterized the design and permitting phase as a necessary initial investment to establish the project’s full scope and cost.

In response to a Councilor’s question about the purpose of a master plan, Mr. Galbraith explained that a comprehensive plan is necessary to determine project costs, evaluate options, and identify opportunities for value engineering before the City and Concord School District can establish an informed cost-sharing arrangement. He noted that the Concord School District had committed $600,000 toward the proposed $1.2 million phase and urged the Council to move forward for the benefit of students and the broader community. He also emphasized the role of organized sports in helping young people develop discipline, engage with supportive adults, and build skills relevant to future employment. In response to Mayor Champlin, Mr. Galbraith confirmed that completing the master plan was a critical step toward determining how project costs should be allocated and supported proceeding with the current phase before finalizing the overall cost-sharing arrangement.

There being no further testimony, Mayor Champlin declared the public hearing closed.

26A. Ordinance amending the Code of Ordinances; Title II, Traffic Code; Chapter 18, Parking, Article 18-1, Stopping, Standing and Parking, Section 18-1-8, Parking Time is Limited in Designated Places, Schedule III, to modify time-limits for parking spaces on the north side of Merrimack Street (Penacook); together with a report from the Assistant Director of Community Development.

Action: City Manager Aspell indicated this request is in conjunction with the adaptive reuse of the former Penacook Branch Library at Merrimack Street. The City and prospective buyer have the property under agreement to be sold and proposing to convert the building into a duplex residential use with one unit on the first floor and another unit on the second floor. The Parking Committee discussed this request and following discussion, the Committee recommends that the time limit on the north side of Merrimack Street in Penacook be amended from two hours to ten hours and enforced Monday through Friday, 7 a.m. To 6 p.m.

Mayor Champlin opened the public hearing. There being no testimony, he declared the hearing closed.

26B. Ordinance amending the Code of Ordinances, Title IV, Zoning Code; Chapter 28, Zoning Ordinance by amending Article 28-7, Access, Circulation, Parking and Loading; together with a report from the Assistant Director of Community Development.

Action: City Manager Aspell turned the next few items over to Assistant Director

of Community Development Tim Thompson.

Assistant Director of Community Development Tim Thompson presented the proposed zoning ordinance amendments, explaining that they would streamline the administration of parking requirements by replacing most parking-related variances before the Zoning Board of Adjustment with conditional use permits and site plan waivers administered by the Planning Board. He stated that the amendments are intended to improve administrative efficiency, provide greater flexibility for development, and reduce the burden on applicants and City staff.

Assistant Director Thompson noted that the amendments complement the Planning Board’s concurrent site plan regulations and incorporate the state requirement limiting residential parking requirements to one space per dwelling unit. In response to Council questions, he confirmed that public notification requirements would remain consistent with existing zoning procedures, including direct notice to abutting property owners by verified mail, that accessible parking requirements would remain unchanged, and that applicants have been able to proceed under either the proposed or existing ordinance since the public hearing notice was posted. The amendments would apply to future projects and applications not yet accepted as complete by the Planning Board. He estimated that the changes could reduce the Zoning Board of Adjustment’s workload by approximately 20 to 50 cases annually.

Mayor Champlin opened the public hearing.

Roy Schweiker, Ward 4 resident, expressed concern that the proposed changes could disproportionately affect lower-income and older residents and favor more expensive housing. He questioned whether the state-mandated limit of one parking space per residential unit adequately reflects actual parking demand and suggested exploring ways to incentivize affordable housing while requiring higher-cost developments to address additional parking and transportation needs. Mr. Schweiker suggested measures included providing additional parking, constructing sidewalks, contributing to public transportation services, funding public parking facilities, and designing subdivision roads to accommodate on-street parking. He also raised concerns about the proposed increase in the allowable length of cul-de-sacs to the state limit, noting potential pedestrian safety risks for children walking to school bus on longer streets without sidewalks. He recommended establishing requirements for sidewalks, bike lanes, or other pedestrian safety measures for longer cul-de-sacs and urged the City to consider policies that support affordable housing while ensuring safe and accessible neighborhood infrastructure.

There being no further testimony, Mayor Champlin declared the public hearing closed.

26C. Ordinance amending the Code of Ordinances, Title IV, Zoning Code; Chapter 28, Zoning Ordinance by amending Article 28-8, Nonconforming Lots, Uses, and Structures, by amending Section 28-8-5 Nonconforming Structures, 28-8-5(d) Removal and Replacement of Certain Nonconforming Residential Structures; together with a report from the Assistant Director of Community Development.

Action: Assistant Director of Community Development Tim Thompson explained

that the proposed amendment would transfer the administration of special exceptions for certain non-conformities to the Planning Board through conditional use permits and eliminate the need for Zoning Board of Adjustment variances when subdivision of a lot renders an existing, unchanged home nonconforming. He stated that the amendment had already eliminated at least three variance applications and was expected to reduce the number of such cases by approximately 10 to 20 or more annually. In response to Council questions, Assistant Director Thompson noted that many downtown properties and smaller lots predate the City’s Zoning Ordinance and do not meet current setback or density requirements. He provided an example of an 1850s-era home on Shaker Road that required a variance solely because a separate portion of the property was being subdivided. Assistant Director Thompson explained that similar provisions or legal interpretations exist in other communities and that the amendment would clarify the City’s approach to these situations.

Councilor Davie agreed that older zoning ordinances often conflict with the existing development patterns of historic town centers and downtowns, and stated that the amendment could help address concerns about the ease of development in Concord. Assistant Director Thompson added that these variances have historically been granted at an approximately 99.9% rate because the affected homes themselves are not changing, and emphasized that the amendment supports the City Council’s goal of making the development process more responsive and efficient.

Mayor Champlin opened the public hearing. There being no testimony, he declared the hearing closed.

26D. Ordinance amending the Code of Ordinances, Title IV, Zoning Code; Chapter 28, Zoning Ordinance by amending Article 28-2-3, The Zoning Map, by amending Section 28-2-3(b)(1); together with a report from the Assistant Director of Community Development.

Action: Assistant Director of Community Development Tim Thompson explained

that the proposed minor textual amendment would update the City's references to the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) Flood Insurance Study and associated flood insurance maps to reflect recently updated federal information. He noted that the City had previously amended these references approximately one year earlier to maintain compliance with the National Flood Insurance Program. He stated that the proposed amendment would ensure continued compliance and preserve resident's ability to access flood insurance.

Mayor Champlin opened the public hearing. There being no testimony, he declared the hearing closed.

26E. Ordinance amending the Code of Ordinances, Title IV, Zoning Code; Chapter 28, Zoning Ordinance by amending Appendix B, List of Arterial Streets and amending Appendix C, List of Collector Streets; together with a report from the Assistant Director of Community Development.

Action: Assistant Director of Community Development Tim Thompson presented

the proposed amendment as a housekeeping update to the City’s Zoning Ordinance glossary to reflect changes in the roadway network and ensure accurate classification of arterial and collector streets, which are subject to different standards and regulatory requirements.

In response to Councilor Brown’s question, Assistant Director Thompson explained that the roadway classifications would not necessarily be reevaluated following completion of the City’s Master Plan, but would instead be reviewed periodically based on growth, traffic volumes, and changing traffic patterns. He further clarified that the proposed changes recognize the existing function of certain streets, including Pleasant Street, Hopkinton Road, and Langley Parkway, by formally designating them as collector roadways where appropriate.

Mayor Champlin opened the public hearing.

Roy Schweiker, resident, expressed concern that the proposed roadway classification amendments were difficult to understand due to the presentation and organization of the changes. He urged the City Manager and staff to ensure future ordinance amendments clearly identify proposed changes and avoid unnecessary duplication or confusing revisions to roadway names and descriptions.

Nicole Fox, resident of Ward 5, speaking in her personal capacity and noting her membership in the Transportation Policy Advisory Committee (TPAC), questioned the rationale for classifying two-lane roads, including Pleasant Street and South Street, as major arterials, citing their multiple land uses and functions beyond moving traffic through the City.

There being no further testimony, Mayor Champlin declared the hearing closed.

26F. Ordinance amending the Code of Ordinances, Title I, General Code, Chapter 8, Fire; together with a report from the City Solicitor.

Action: City Solicitor John Conforti and Fire Chief John Chisholm addressed the Council regarding Items 26F and 26G, explaining that the two proposed ordinances were related and would need to be considered and approved or denied together. City Solicitor Conforti explained that the amendments would reorganize the City’s existing fire, building, and housing maintenance and occupancy code provisions into separate sections and make housekeeping revisions to align with state-adopted codes. The amendments would remove duplicative provisions and language inconsistent with state requirements and place the applicable regulations within their appropriate chapters of the City Code.

Mayor Champlin opened the public hearing. There being no testimony, he declared the hearing closed.

26G. Ordinance amending the Code of Ordinances, Title III, Building and Housing

26H. Resolution appropriating the sum of $23,397 for Law Enforcement Related

Programs and accepting the sum of $23,397 in Unmatched Grant Funds from the United States Department of Justice Edward Byrne Memorial Justice Assistance grant program for this purpose; together with a report from the Deputy Chief of Police.

Action: City Manager Aspell presented the grant program, explaining that it

provides funding for technological upgrades, equipment purchases, and specialized training for department personnel, with no local matching funds required. He stated that the City would enter into a Memorandum of Understanding with Merrimack County regarding the allocation and use of funds, with $18,397 allocated to the Concord Police Department and $5,000 to Merrimack County.

Interim Deputy Police Chief Patrick (PJ) O’Frias explained that the grant application, submitted by Deputy Chief Steve Smagula prior to his retirement, would fund Graykey technology for cell phone investigations, potentially including specialized training for the Police Department’s computer crimes unit, as well as breaching equipment such as ballistic shields and breaching tools. The County’s allocation would support upgrades to patrol equipment for its deputies. Interim Deputy O’Frias clarified that the application specifically identified these technology and equipment needs, and that any future use of the funds for other purposes would require an appropriate request and approval process.

Chris Levesque, resident of Ward 9, expressed concern regarding the Police Department’s proposed use of grant funding for breaching equipment and suggested that the funds would be better spent purchasing body cameras to promote officer accountability when mistakes occur.

35. Resolution appropriating the sum of $1,200,000 in the Memorial Field Project (CIP

#557) for Final Design and Permitting, authorizing the issuance of General Obligation Bonds and Notes in the sum of $600,000, and accepting the sum of $600,000 in donations from the Concord School District for this purpose; together with a report from the Parks and Recreation Director. (Public testimony received.)

Action: Councilor Fennessy moved approval of the Resolution. The motion was

duly seconded by Councilor Grady Sexton.

Councilor Kurtz expressed support for the $1.2 million appropriation for Memorial Field and urged the Council to direct staff to begin work immediately on a Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) with the Concord School Board. She acknowledged the longstanding tensions between the City Council and Concord School Board, as well as historical distrust between Concord and Penacook, but emphasized that these issues should not delay a project benefiting local children and the broader community. Councilor Kurtz recognized the City's financial challenges and the burden of deferred maintenance but stressed the importance of establishing a more collaborative working relationship with Concord School District and ensuring that Penacook residents feel adequately represented. She stated that she would not support additional appropriations for Memorial Field beyond the current $1.2 million unless a clear agreement between the City Council and Concord School Board was established through an MOU.

Councilor Horne acknowledged the need for immediate repairs to Memorial Field but questioned whether the City should proceed with the proposed $22 million sports complex before establishing its affordability and resolving outstanding responsibilities with the Concord School District. Citing concerns about costly design investments in projects that may ultimately prove unaffordable, she emphasized the need to establish a Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) before committing substantial additional funds.

Councilor Horne stated that the MOU should clearly define ownership, financial obligations, operational control, maintenance, scheduling, public access, revenue sharing, and dispute resolution. She cited the Rundlett School traffic rerouting issue as an example of the potential costs and complications resulting from insufficient coordination between the City and Concord School District. She also raised concerns about the cumulative impact of debt service, school bond obligations, property taxes, and revaluations on residents, particularly those already experiencing financial hardship. She questioned whether the proposed project was an appropriate priority given residents’ basic needs and reductions in City services.

Councilor Horne requested that the City and Concord School District identify their respective financial commitments and develop projections covering construction, operations, maintenance, future capital replacements, and anticipated revenues. She urged the Council to address immediate repairs, establish an equitable agreement between the City and Concord School District, and determine what the community could reasonably afford before authorizing further design expenditures. She also referenced a petition signed by nearly 500 community members seeking a clear resolution and emphasized transparency and fiscal responsibility.

Councilor Fennessey noted that Memorial Field is currently a City-owned asset, with the City bearing full responsibility for its maintenance, liabilities, and associated costs. He stated that relations and cooperation between the City Council and Concord School District had improved during his tenure, citing the District’s financial contribution toward the initial design work and its current $600,000 contribution toward the project. He noted that accepting financial support from the Concord School District would likely require negotiating an MOU that addresses shared responsibilities and the extent of the District’s involvement in facility decisions.

Councilor Fennessey stated that while the proposed $22 million conceptual plan includes approximately $5.5 million for new buildings that may not be constructed, the initial focus has been on improvements to the fields and track. He explained that addressing longstanding drainage problems would require extensive work on all fields and would involve multimillion-dollar costs, rather than minor repairs alone. He also noted that the project had been scaled back from an initial conceptual estimate of $36 million following numerous meetings and consideration of alternative plans.

Councilor Fennessey emphasized that the condition of Memorial Field requires attention and framed the current decision as whether to proceed with the initial phase of work in partnership with the Concord School District, which has indicated its willingness to contribute funding. He expressed support for moving forward while acknowledging that the decision rested with the Council.

Councilor Schultz expressed concern that state and federal economic and tax policies place a disproportionate financial burden on working-class, middle-class, and lower-income residents, as well as municipalities and school districts. She stated that those with greater financial resources should bear a larger share of public expenses and expressed support for investing in programs and projects benefiting children and residents in need. However, she noted that competing community needs and residents’ financial hardships informed his position. Councilor Schultz stated that, in representing Ward 9 and reflecting the concerns of constituents struggling financially, she could not support the appropriation at this time and would vote against it.

Councilor Brown thanked Councilors Horne, Schultz, Fennessey, and Kurtz for their remarks and acknowledged the compelling testimony received from residents. She emphasized the importance of investing in children and stated that additional time was needed to consider the concerns and suggestions raised during the meeting. She suggested postponing a decision until the following month to allow time to develop a Memorandum of Understanding with the Concord School District. Councilor Brown questioned the City's spending priorities, contrasting investments in the Beaver Meadow golf clubhouse and golf course improvements with the lack of adequate facilities for student track practices. She urged the Council to prioritize children and reconsider the allocation of public resources. She also expressed conditional support for the Memorial Field project but stated that she would not support the motion without an MOU. She also supported Mr. Washburn's referenced suggestion to issue a Request for Proposals (RFP) and urged the Council to consider restoring the Golf Fund to an enterprise fund, noting that the $831,000 burden on Concord taxpayers could instead be supported by golf course users. She encouraged the Council to revisit the matter the following month with a focus on advancing the project and addressing the outstanding concerns.

Councilor Fennessey asked Councilor Brown whether she would support the project if an MOU were established. Councilor Brown clarified that she would also want an RFP for construction services and stated that, although she would consider supporting future construction appropriations if an MOU and RFP were in place, she could not commit to supporting the project without first reviewing the terms of the MOU.

Councilor Todd expressed agreement with Councilor Horne’s concerns regarding the need for additional information before proceeding. He supported beginning discussions with the Concord School District as soon as practicable but stated that he would not be comfortable negotiating a final MOU without sufficient data to evaluate the project’s costs, anticipated usage, and equitable cost-sharing between Concord and Penacook residents. He noted that decisions regarding field surfaces, including turf versus natural grass, could affect usage levels and Concord School District’s future use of the facility.

Councilor Todd thanked the committee, Councilors Fennessey and Foote, Parks and Recreation staff, and others involved in developing the plan. He noted that the current $22 million estimate represented a 27% reduction from the earlier estimate and expressed optimism that further design and planning could result in additional cost reductions. He looked forward to reviewing updated cost estimates and plans as the process continued.

Councilor Foote expressed support for the appropriation, emphasizing the benefits of youth sports and the importance of providing adequate athletic facilities in the capital city. He noted that he and Councilor Fennessey had participated in approximately 10 meetings reviewing project options and stated that continued temporary repairs had contributed to the facility’s current condition. Councilor Foote supported establishing an MOU with the Concord School District before authorizing any additional expenditures beyond the current $1.2 million appropriation. He acknowledged that additional data would be needed to inform future decisions and expressed hope that the Council would approve the measure and advance the project.

Councilor Keach expressed support for the appropriation, stating that Memorial Field requires repairs regardless of whether an agreement with Concord School District is ultimately reached. He questioned why the City would forgo the Concord School District’s $600,000 contribution and supported proceeding with the design work to establish project costs and requirements before negotiating the longer-term agreement.

Councilor Schlosser supported the appropriation and emphasized the need for an MOU that establishes a fair allocation of costs between Concord and Penacook residents and Concord School District. He stated that the City needed reliable cost estimates to inform those discussions and agreed that no additional appropriations should be made until project costs and cost-sharing responsibilities were clearly established.

Councilor Davie stated that he would reluctantly support the appropriation but expressed reservations about an eventual 50-50 cost-sharing arrangement. He urged staff to pursue available grants and other outside funding opportunities and suggested that the Joint Committee consider initiating a capital campaign.

Councilor Kalob stated that she would reluctantly support the appropriation but expressed concern about bonding the City’s $600,000 share and the long-term financial implications of the project. Referencing a 2012 report identifying concerns with the bleachers and drainage, she noted that recommended improvements had not been completed and emphasized the need to address the consequences of deferred maintenance. She stated that her support extended only to the current $1.2 million appropriation and called for an MOU, specific information on grant opportunities, a framework and funding goal for a capital campaign, and exploration of public-private partnerships. She also questioned whether the City would have the capacity to operate and maintain the facility responsibly over the long term.

Councilor Brown asked whether the City’s year-end budget surplus was known. City Manager Aspell responded that the surplus following June 30 had not yet been determined.

Mayor Champlin explained that the resolution before the Council authorized bonding for the $1.2 million appropriation. He noted that the City Manager had identified available reserve funds and impact fees as potential alternative funding sources. He explained that using Recreation Reserve funds for the Memorial Field project could reduce the funds available for other obligations, including debt service associated with the Community Center and Beaver Meadow clubhouse. The Mayor invited Council discussion regarding whether to proceed with the proposed bonding or use a combination of bonding, impact fees, and other available funds.

Councilor Sekou emphasized the importance of addressing safety concerns at Memorial Field, particularly those affecting children. Referring to the presentation and public testimony, he noted that local student-athletes had to travel to other communities to participate in sports and that some talented students had left the community because they felt insufficiently supported. He restated the Council’s priority of public safety and described its importance from his perspective as a parent.

Councilor Sekou reiterated his support for the appropriation, emphasizing that the funding would support project design rather than commit the City to full construction. He highlighted the benefits of youth sports, including opportunities for student-athletes to excel and represent Concord. He stated that his support was intended to advance the design process and help position the project for grant funding. Councilor Sekou also emphasized that an MOU between the City and Concord School District must be required before any additional appropriations beyond the current $1.2 million.

Councilor Kurtz asked City Manager Aspell to clarify the source of approximately $140,000 in available Capital Project Funds. He explained that the amount was anticipated to remain from funds previously allocated for bleacher removal, although the project had not yet been fully closed out.

City Manager Aspell cautioned that using available reserves, impact fees, or remaining project funds would reduce the City's financial flexibility for future obligations and could increase pressure on the tax rate or require service reductions. He explained that the Council should focus on whether to proceed with the design and be prepared to consider a capital project, rather than on which funding account would be used. He noted that design work would also support grant applications and negotiations with Concord School District.

City Manager Aspell cited the Citywide Community Center as an example of a successful partnership established through an MOU between the City and Concord School District. He also cautioned that projected facility revenues may not fully offset operating and construction costs over time, potentially leaving taxpayers responsible for those expenses.

Councilor Fennessey asked whether any available impact fees would expire if not used immediately. City Manager Aspell confirmed that none were scheduled to expire and explained that impact fees could potentially be reserved to offset the City's share of future bond payments, reducing the project's impact on the tax rate.

Councilor Kalob acknowledged the financial implications of using reserve funds but emphasized that the method of financing was an important consideration. She noted that reduced financial flexibility could be an acceptable consequence of using available funds rather than bonding.

Mayor Champlin paused discussion to entertain a motion to suspend the rules to continue the meeting beyond 11:00 p.m. Councilor Kretovic moved to suspend the rules to continue the meeting after 11:00 p.m. The motion was duly seconded by Councilor Schultz and passed with the required two-thirds majority.

Councilor Schultz asked about the City's experience with capital campaigns and whether St. Paul's School had been approached regarding potential support for the project. City Manager Aspell explained that capital campaigns had previously been conducted by private groups in partnership with the City, citing White Park Playground and Merrimack Lodge as examples. He described an arrangement in which the City committed funding while private groups raised additional contributions, noting that alternative funding sources and available year-end surpluses had sometimes reduced the need for bonding. He also clarified that St. Paul's School pays property taxes on properties subject to taxation under state law.

Councilor Foote expressed reservations about bonding the appropriation when other funding sources might be available, citing interest and transaction costs associated with borrowing. He indicated that he would support using available funds from existing accounts instead of issuing bonds, if a motion to that effect were made.

Councilor Todd acknowledged City Manager Aspell's experience in managing municipal projects and historical knowledge of prior funding arrangements. Regarding the proposed financing, he favored preserving available reserves and other funding sources to maintain flexibility during preparation of the FY2028 budget, which he anticipated would present significant financial challenges.

Councilor Todd moved the question. The motion was duly seconded by Councilor Grady Sexton and passed.

Mayor Champlin requested the vote on the original motion.

Councilor Schultz requested a roll-call vote to ensure the public record clearly reflected each Councilor’s vote. Mayor Champlin stated the vote had already started. Councilor Schultz objected that the initial vote had begun before all Councilors had an opportunity to respond and asked that the vote be conducted again for fairness and transparency. The Mayor referenced parliamentary procedure.

Councilor Fennessey then offered a motion to reconsider the vote in the interest of time. The motion was duly seconded by Councilor Kretovic.

Councilor Schultz requested a roll call vote.

Roll Call:

NO - Councilor Schultz, Councilor Brown, Councilor Horne,

YES - Councilor Sekou, Councilor Todd, Mayor Champlin, Councilor Davie, Councilor Fennessy, Councilor Foote, Councilor Grady-Sexton, Councilor Kalob, Councilor Keach, Counselor Kretovic, Counselor Kurtz, Counselor Schlosser

The motion passed by the necessary two-thirds majority.

7. Ordinance amending the Code of Ordinances; Title II, Traffic Code; Chapter 17, Vehicles and Traffic, Article 17-6, Miscellaneous Rules, by adding Section 17-6-12, Noyes Street and Cypress Streets - Restricted Access During School Drop-Off/Pick-Up Hours; together with a communication from John F. Weaver, McLane Middleton. (Reports from the City Solicitor and the Transportation Engineer submitted).

Action: Councilor Kretovic moved to set the item for a December Public Hearing.

The motion was duly seconded by Councilor Grady Sexton.

Councilor Kretovic urged the Council to move forward with consideration of an ordinance addressing traffic patterns around the new Rundlett Middle School. She expressed concern that the proposed traffic arrangements prioritized parent pickup over the safety and mobility of children who walk or bike to school from nearby neighborhoods. She noted that neighborhood streets had long been shared by residents and students and cited other schools where parent pickup had been managed without similar neighborhood disruption. She suggested that the City Solicitor review the ordinance and requested that it be scheduled for consideration in December.

Councilor Sekou asked whether referral to the City Solicitor was being proposed as a formal recommendation or as a suggestion. Councilor Kretovic clarified that it was a suggestion and reiterated her preference for consideration in December.

Councilor Schlosser acknowledged residents’ concerns regarding traffic and neighborhood impacts but noted that the proposed traffic plan had undergone review by the Concord School Board, City Council, engineers, and advisory committees. He emphasized the potential safety benefits of separating parent and bus traffic and recommended referring the ordinance to the City Solicitor and the Transportation Policy Advisory Committee (TPAC) for further review before scheduling a public hearing.

Councilor Fennessey requested clarification regarding the proposed schedule, confirming that the matter would be noticed in November for a public hearing in December.

Councilor Grady-Sexton supported scheduling a public hearing, stating that the Council had already received substantial technical input and that further referrals could delay a decision affecting neighborhood safety and quality of life. She emphasized that identifying the safest available alternative did not necessarily establish that the proposed arrangement was safe and urged the Council to hear directly from the community. She expressed support for the ordinance.

Councilor Kurtz asked whether the City Solicitor and relevant committees could review the ordinance in time to provide recommendations before the December public hearing. The City Solicitor indicated that his office could review the matter but could not guarantee the other committees’ schedules.

Councilor Schultz stated that, in her view, the Council had already conducted substantial due diligence and heard extensive public testimony on the traffic concerns.

Councilor Todd supported holding a public hearing but recommended that the ordinance first be referred to the City Solicitor, TPAC, and the Traffic Operations Committee (TOC). He raised concerns regarding the ordinance’s legality, enforceability, and practical application, including how restrictions on parent traffic would be implemented. He stated that the relevant committees could provide additional technical and operational guidance.

Councilor Davie stated that he did not support the ordinance as written but favored further discussion, whether through the Council or the relevant committees.

Councilor Foote supported moving the matter to a public hearing, noting that TPAC had conducted an extensive review and heard significant public input. He referenced his experience with Rundlett Middle School and his participation in the TPAC discussion, including a question about whether pedestrian-vehicle conflicts had previously been reported. He expressed concern that the proposed ordinance could create problems that did not currently exist and urged the Council to proceed without further unnecessary delay. He also cited traffic concerns associated with other school projects.

Councilor Grady-Sexton reiterated that delaying a decision was itself consequential and urged the Council to act rather than continue postponing the matter.

Mayor Champlin expressed reservations about advancing an ordinance without review by the appropriate legal and advisory bodies. He distinguished review of the specific ordinance from earlier discussions of general traffic patterns and stated that he would support scheduling a December public hearing, provided the ordinance was referred to the City Solicitor, TPAC, and TOC for

- recommendations beforehand.

Councilor Kretovic clarified that the proposed ordinance concerned traffic restrictions and that the conversation was not around sidewalks on Noyes Street and Cypress Street. She stated that the neighborhood’s concerns arose from the proposed traffic changes without sidewalks and emphasized that the discussion should focus on the ordinance rather than reopen broader decisions regarding school traffic design. The Mayor confirmed that the proposed referrals would concern the ordinance itself.

Councilor Schultz moved the question, and the motion was seconded by Councilor Fennessey. The motion passed by the required two-thirds majority.

The Council then voted on Councilor Kretovic’s original motion to schedule the ordinance for a public hearing. The motion failed.

Mayor Champlin subsequently moved to notice the ordinance in November for a public hearing in December, with referrals to the City Solicitor’s Office, TPAC, and TOC. The motion was seconded by Councilor Grady-Sexton.

During further discussion, Councilor Schlosser asked whether adverse findings regarding the ordinance’s legality or enforceability would affect the scheduled public hearing. The Mayor clarified that the committees’ and City Solicitor’s recommendations would be presented for the Council’s consideration in December. Councilor Sekou asked whether the referrals could be completed in time, and the Mayor expressed the expectation that they could.

Councilor Schultz noted that the proposed ordinance had originated with outside legal counsel and characterized the referrals as an opportunity to ensure that the City’s legal and operational concerns were addressed.

Councilor Grady-Sexton supported the revised motion and expressed concern that neighborhood residents had felt compelled to retain legal counsel to bring their concerns forward. She emphasized the stress experienced by the neighborhood and sought assurance that the relevant committee review could occur before December. Councilor Todd indicated that the referral should allow the matter to be considered by the appropriate committee in time for the scheduled hearing.

Mayor Champlin's motion passed with one dissenting vote.

22. Report from Councilor Kretovic, Rules Committee Chair, recommending

proposed changes to the Rules of the City Council by adopting an Ethics Complaint Form. (Pulled from consent by Councilor Brown.)

Action: Councilor Kurtz moved approval of the report. The motion was duly

seconded by Councilor Todd.

Councilor Brown addressed the voluntary ethics complaint form recommended by the Rules Committee. She stated that the form provides useful guidance for documenting complaints, including dates, locations, patterns of conduct, supporting evidence, and applicable provisions of the Code of Ethics, but does not amend Ordinance 30-3-29 or preclude residents from submitting complaints in other formats that satisfy the ordinance's requirements.

She noted that only three of the Rules Committee's five members attended the meeting at which the form was advanced and expressed concern that meeting accessibility and scheduling had not been discussed. She raised concerns regarding potential conflicts of interest involving members of the committee.

Councilor Schultz moved the question. The motion was duly seconded by Councilor Keach and passed with one dissenting vote.

The original motion passed with one dissenting vote.

Comments, Requests by Mayor, City Councilors

Councilor Todd thanked Sweet Dreams Ice Cream, Irene Ortega, and the volunteers who organized the first Fall Festival, expressing hope that the event would continue in future years. He announced upcoming Penacook Historical Society events, including its annual Halloween celebration on October 24 from 1:00 to 3:00 p.m. at the 1834 Rolfe House on Penacook Street, featuring a free, all-ages costume parade and community celebration. He reminded residents that Penacook trick-or-treating would take place October 30 from 5:00 to 7:30 p.m., and Concord trick-or-treating would take place October 31 during the same hours. He also announced a community potluck dinner on November 6 featuring guest speaker Aaron Moulton, who would discuss researching the history of one’s home. The event is sponsored by New Hampshire Humanities.

Councilor Kretovic congratulated City Manager Aspell on being named Citizen of the Year and noted that the celebration would take place on November 4, 2026.

Councilor Davie thanked the Community Development Department and its consultants for the Master Plan workshop held in September, commending the presentations and staff participation. He encouraged residents to vote in November.

Councilor Schultz wished the City Clerk and staff well in preparing for Election Day on November 3 and encouraged residents to vote. She also expressed opposition to the second ballot measure, which she personally referred to as a “tax trap.”

Councilor Fennessy echoed Councilor Schultz’s remarks, thanking the City Clerk’s Office in advance for its work and expressing confidence in the staff’s preparations for Election Day.

Councilor Brown announced an event scheduled for Friday, October 30, from 6:00 to 7:00 p.m., featuring four historical figures associated with Concord and New Hampshire in recognition of the nation’s 250th anniversary. The participants would speak about their historical significance and how these figures’ legacies are reflected in their own work and daily lives.

Councilor Foote recognized October as Breast Cancer Awareness Month and encouraged residents to seek routine cancer screenings. He also encouraged eligible residents to donate blood platelets. He congratulated Concord resident Rich Rosato on completing his tenure as President of the American Dental Association, expressing appreciation for his service.

Mayor Champlin reminded Council members to silence their cell phones and use them judiciously during meetings to maintain appropriate decorum, referencing an accidental phone disturbance during a previous meeting’s Councilor’s commemoration of the September 11 anniversary. He noted that sample ballots were available on the City’s website, noting October 26 was the final day to register to vote before the election, and reminding residents that absentee ballots were available. He also reminded residents that voter registration would be available at the polls. Finally, he congratulated Merrimack Valley High School football on its 6-0 record and wished the team success in its upcoming game.

Comments, Requests by the City Manager

Adjournment

Action: Councilor Kretovic moved to adjourn the meeting at 11:37 p.m. The

motion was duly seconded by Councilor Kurtz and passed unanimously.
